title: Mini Project: Bank Account
summary: Synthesize all constructor concepts — default, parameterized, overloaded, this, and constructor chaining — to build a complete Bank Account Management System.
learningObjectives: Design and build an industry-style BankAccount class from scratch
Implement overloaded constructors with safe default fallbacks
Apply 'this(...)' constructor chaining to centralize validation and balance initialization
Combine constructors with deposit and display methods to manage multiple client accounts
expectedOutcomes: A production-ready Bank Account Java application built progressively
Deep confidence in architecting real-world classes with flexible construction workflows

analogy.headline: A real bank onboard different customers through different application channels
analogy.story:
When people open accounts at a commercial bank, they arrive through different channels:

1. **Online Instant Registration:** A user signs up with their name and email, but hasn't deposited money yet ($0.0 balance).
2. **Branch Walk-in with Minimum Opening Deposit:** A customer visits the branch with their name, account number, and deposits $500 cash.
3. **VIP Platinum Client:** An executive opens an account with an existing account ID and a $10,000 opening bonus.

All three people walk away with a valid `BankAccount` object. But the bank needs flexible constructor entry points and centralized validation to ensure no account is opened in an illegal or broken state!

In this guided project, you will build this complete system step-by-step.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Real-world enterprise systems rely on constructor overloading and chaining to accommodate diverse onboarding pathways while guaranteeing data integrity.

activities.title: System Architecture & 10-Step Guided Build Blueprint

keyTakeaways: Step 1-2: Define BankAccount with accountHolder, accountNumber, and balance fields
Step 3: Master constructor initializing all 3 fields with non-negative balance validation
Step 4-5: Overload constructors for partial data (holder + number only, or default guest)
Step 6-7: Chain all constructors to the master constructor using this(...)
Step 8-10: Implement deposit(), withdraw(), and displaySummary() methods to verify multi-account isolation

activities.content:
### The 10-Step Guided Build Path:

```text
Step 1 ──► Define BankAccount class
Step 2 ──► Declare fields: accountHolder (String), accountNumber (String), balance (double)
Step 3 ──► Create Master Constructor: (holder, number, balance)
Step 4 ──► Add Balance Validation: if opening balance < 0, clamp to 0.0
Step 5 ──► Create 2-parameter Constructor: (holder, number) -> chains to master with balance = 0.0
Step 6 ──► Create No-arg Constructor: () -> chains to 2-arg constructor with ("Guest User", "PENDING-000")
Step 7 ──► Add deposit(double amount) method to mutate balance
Step 8 ──► Add displayAccount() method to format account card
Step 9 ──► Instantiate 3 accounts in Main: Default, Zero-Balance, and Funded VIP
Step 10 ─► Perform transactions and verify data isolation across all 3 accounts
```

### Architectural Design Diagram:
```text
[ BankAccount() ]
       │  chains via this("Guest User", "PENDING-000")
       ▼
[ BankAccount(holder, number) ]
       │  chains via this(holder, number, 0.0)
       ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [ BankAccount(holder, number, balance) ]  ◄── MASTER   │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ • Validates: balance >= 0                              │
│ • Assigns: this.accountHolder = holder                 │
│ • Assigns: this.accountNumber = number                 │
│ • Assigns: this.balance = balance                      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

activities.title: The Complete Bank Account Architecture in Java
activities.description: Notice how all three construction paths converge cleanly into the master constructor. Changes to account validation or formatting only ever need to be made in one place.

questions.prompt: Why is constructor chaining especially valuable in a financial class like BankAccount?
options: It prevents the program from requiring internet access
It ensures security checks and non-negative balance validation are executed through one single master constructor, eliminating bypass loopholes
It automatically connects to the bank's SQL database
It converts all balances into cryptocurrencies
questions.explanation: Routing all constructors to a master constructor ensures validation rules can never be bypassed by alternative creation paths.

questions.prompt: If a user calls 'new BankAccount("Alice", "ACC-101")' in our project, which constructor executes first?
options: The no-arg constructor
The 2-argument constructor, which immediately delegates to the 3-argument master constructor via this(...)
The deposit method
The garbage collector
questions.explanation: Java invokes the 2-arg constructor, whose first statement is this(holder, number, 0.0), delegating to the master constructor.

questions.prompt: What happens in our project if someone passes an opening balance of -$500.0?
options: The bank balance is set to -$500.0
The constructor's validation logic clamps the balance to 0.0
The JVM terminates immediately
The compiler refuses to compile
questions.explanation: The master constructor checks: if (balance < 0.0) this.balance = 0.0;, preventing negative starting balances.

hints.hint: Check the validation logic in the master constructor.

questions.prompt: Why do we use 'this.accountHolder = accountHolder;' inside the constructor?
options: To resolve variable shadowing between the parameter 'accountHolder' and instance field 'accountHolder'
Because Java requires 'this' before every single variable in the class
To encrypt the customer's name
To delete the temporary parameter from RAM
questions.explanation: 'this' explicitly routes the parameter value into the instance's field.

questions.prompt: If Account 1 deposits $500, what happens to Account 2's balance?
options: Account 2 also gets $500 because they share the BankAccount class
Account 2's balance is completely unchanged because each object has separate, isolated memory in the heap
Account 2's balance is reset to 0.0
Both accounts combine into one single account
questions.explanation: Objects have independent state. Mutating Account 1 has zero effect on Account 2.

questions.prompt: Can you call 'displayAccount()' before making any deposits?
options: Yes, because the constructor has already guaranteed that all fields were properly initialized
No, you must call deposit at least once
Only if the balance is greater than 100
No, methods cannot be called until main returns
questions.explanation: Constructors guarantee that from the moment of instantiation, the object is 100% valid and ready for method calls.

questions.prompt: Why did we NOT make the fields 'private' in this module?
options: Because private fields are illegal in Java
Because private fields, getters, and setters belong to Module 3 (Encapsulation), preserving clean step-by-step learning
Because private fields make code run slower
Because constructors cannot access private fields
questions.explanation: LearnBySelf adheres to strict pedagogical boundaries. Encapsulation and access modifiers are taught thoroughly in Module 3.

questions.prompt: What would happen if we removed 'BankAccount()' no-arg constructor from our project?
options: Calling 'new BankAccount()' in main would cause a compile-time error: constructor BankAccount() is undefined
Java would automatically supply the default constructor anyway
All existing accounts would be deleted
The class would become abstract
questions.explanation: Because custom constructors exist, the compiler suppresses the default constructor. Removing BankAccount() breaks callers using no-arg creation.

hints.hint: Remember the vanishing default constructor rule.

questions.prompt: Which OOP concept is demonstrated by having 3 constructors in BankAccount?
options: Inheritance
Constructor Overloading
Polymorphic Interface Implementation
Package Encapsulation
questions.explanation: Having multiple constructors with different parameter lists in the same class is constructor overloading.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of the 'deposit(double amount)' method vs the constructor?
options: Constructor births and initializes the account; deposit mutates the balance during the account's active lifetime
Deposit creates the account; constructor deletes it
They do the exact same thing with different syntax
Deposit can only be called from inside the constructor
questions.explanation: Constructors handle initial state at birth; methods handle operational state changes throughout the object's life.

interviewQA.question: Walk me through how you architected the constructors in your Bank Account system.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: I designed a 3-tier constructor hierarchy: 1) A master constructor taking accountHolder, accountNumber, and balance, which validates the opening balance and performs all field assignments, 2) A 2-argument constructor for standard onboarding that chains into the master constructor with a default 0.0 balance, and 3) A no-arg constructor that chains into the 2-arg constructor with placeholder guest credentials. This centralized all initialization and prevented code duplication.
keyPoints: Master constructor handles validation and assignments
DRY principle enforced across all construction paths
commonMistakes: Duplicating validation logic across every constructor rather than using this().

interviewQA.question: How did you ensure that an account cannot be initialized with a negative balance?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Inside the master constructor, I placed a validation check: if the passed balance is less than zero, it is clamped to 0.0. Because all other overloaded constructors chain into this master constructor via 'this(...)', this rule is impossible to bypass regardless of which constructor the caller invokes.
keyPoints: Chaining ensures no constructor bypasses validation
Guarantees valid state upon completion of 'new'
commonMistakes: Placing validation only in the 3-arg constructor without chaining the others to it.

interviewQA.question: Why did you use 'this.accountHolder = accountHolder;' instead of renaming the parameter?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Using 'this' to resolve variable shadowing is the idiomatic standard in Java. It allows parameter names to remain meaningful and descriptive in documentation and IDE auto-complete, while explicitly identifying the instance variable target.
commonMistakes: Using artificial prefixes like aHolder or myName.

interviewQA.question: What is the consequence of adding parameterized constructors if callers still need a no-arg constructor?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Once a parameterized constructor is declared, Java suppresses the automatic default constructor. If callers still need to create blank or default objects with 'new BankAccount()', the developer must explicitly define a no-arg constructor.
keyPoints: Must provide explicit no-arg constructor for no-argument instantiation
commonMistakes: Forgetting that Java removes the default constructor once any constructor is written.

interviewQA.question: What would happen if you tried to log a message before 'this(...)' in one of your chained constructors?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: It would cause a compilation error. Java strictly requires 'this(...)' or 'super(...)' to be the first statement inside a constructor body to ensure that object state is established before any other statements are evaluated.
keyPoints: Compile error: 'Constructor call must be the first statement'
Ensures object is constructed before side-effects execute
commonMistakes: Thinking you can execute print statements prior to this().

interviewQA.question: How does this BankAccount system prove that objects in Java maintain independent memory state?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: When we instantiate three different accounts (acc1, acc2, acc3) in Main and call deposit() on acc2, only acc2's balance increases. acc1 and acc3 retain their original balances. This demonstrates that each object has its own dedicated heap memory allocation.
keyPoints: Mutating one object does not affect sibling instances
commonMistakes: Confusing instance fields with static class variables.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between writing business logic in constructors versus in methods?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Constructors should only contain logic necessary to establish an initial valid state (such as assigning fields and validating incoming arguments). Ongoing operations, repeated calculations, and state changes (such as depositing, withdrawing, or generating statements) belong in methods.
commonMistakes: Overloading constructors with long-running business logic.

activities.title: Module 2 Mastery Checkpoint (10-Point Checklist)
checklist: I understand why constructors exist and how they execute automatically during 'new'.
I know the two golden rules: exact class name and zero return type.
I understand the difference between the compiler's default constructor and an explicit no-arg constructor.
I know that declaring any custom constructor removes the automatic default constructor.
I can write parameterized constructors to enforce required object data at birth.
I can overload constructors to support multiple object creation workflows.
I understand variable shadowing and how 'this.field = field' resolves it.
I can chain constructors using 'this(...)' to keep my code DRY.
I know that 'this(...)' must always be the very first statement in a constructor.
I have built a complete, working Bank Account system combining all of these concepts.

practiceProblems.title: Build the Core BankAccount Class
practiceProblems.description:
Step 1 & 2 of our guided project:

• Create `BankAccount` with `String accountHolder`, `String accountNumber`, and `double balance`.
• Add Master Constructor `BankAccount(String accountHolder, String accountNumber, double balance)` using `this` to assign fields.
• Add `void displayInfo()` that prints: `[accountHolder] ([accountNumber]) - $[balance]`.
• In `Main`, create an account for `"Dev Sharma"`, `"ACC-999"`, `500.0` and call `displayInfo()`.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Step 1 & 2 of our guided project:

• Create `BankAccount` with `String accountHolder`, `String accountNumber`, and `double balance`.
• Add Master Constructor `BankAccount(String accountHolder, String accountNumber, double balance)` using `this` to assign fields.
• Add `void displayInfo()` that prints: `[accountHolder] ([accountNumber]) - $[balance]`.
• In `Main`, create an account for `"Dev Sharma"`, `"ACC-999"`, `500.0` and call `displayInfo()`.
practiceProblems.hint: Assign all 3 fields with this.field = field; in the constructor.
hints: In main, create new BankAccount("Dev Sharma", "ACC-999", 500.0).

practiceProblems.title: Add Negative Balance Clamping
practiceProblems.description:
Step 3: Enhance the master constructor to sanitize negative opening balances:

• If `balance < 0.0`, clamp `this.balance = 0.0;`.
• In `Main`, create `acc = new BankAccount("Karan", "ACC-123", -250.0);`.
• Call `displayInfo()` to verify output: `Karan (ACC-123) - $0.0`.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Step 3: Enhance the master constructor to sanitize negative opening balances:

• In `Main`, create `acc = new BankAccount("Karan", "ACC-123", -250.0);`.
• Call `displayInfo()` to verify output: `Karan (ACC-123) - $0.0`.
hints: Always guard against invalid starting balances.

practiceProblems.title: Add Constructor Chaining for Default Accounts
practiceProblems.description:
Step 4 & 5: Add constructor overloading with chaining:

• `BankAccount(String holder, String number)` chains to master with `balance = 0.0`.
• `BankAccount()` chains to 2-arg constructor with `"Guest User"` and `"PENDING-000"`.
• In `Main`, instantiate with `new BankAccount()` and call `displayInfo()`: `Guest User (PENDING-000) - $0.0`.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Step 4 & 5: Add constructor overloading with chaining:

• `BankAccount(String holder, String number)` chains to master with `balance = 0.0`.
• `BankAccount()` chains to 2-arg constructor with `"Guest User"` and `"PENDING-000"`.
• In `Main`, instantiate with `new BankAccount()` and call `displayInfo()`: `Guest User (PENDING-000) - $0.0`.
practiceProblems.hint: BankAccount(String h, String n) { this(h, n, 0.0); } and BankAccount() { this("Guest User", "PENDING-000"); }
hints: Constructor calls must be the first line.

practiceProblems.title: Implement Deposit and Withdrawal Operations
practiceProblems.description:
Step 6 & 7: Add transaction methods to our chained BankAccount class:

• Method `void deposit(double amount)`: if `amount > 0`, adds to `balance`.
• Method `boolean withdraw(double amount)`: if `amount > 0 && amount <= balance`, subtracts from `balance` and returns `true`; else returns `false`.
• In `Main`, start with $100.0, deposit $50.0, withdraw $30.0, and print: `Final Balance: $120.0`.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Step 6 & 7: Add transaction methods to our chained BankAccount class:

• Method `void deposit(double amount)`: if `amount > 0`, adds to `balance`.
• Method `boolean withdraw(double amount)`: if `amount > 0 && amount <= balance`, subtracts from `balance` and returns `true`; else returns `false`.
• In `Main`, start with $100.0, deposit $50.0, withdraw $30.0, and print: `Final Balance: $120.0`.
hints: balance += amount for deposit; balance -= amount for withdraw.

practiceProblems.title: Simulate Multi-Account Branch Isolation
practiceProblems.description:
Step 8, 9 & 10: Run the complete multi-account branch test:

• Account 1: `new BankAccount()`
• Account 2: `new BankAccount("Rahul", "ACC-101")`
• Account 3: `new BankAccount("Priya", "ACC-202", 500.0)`

Perform operations:
• `acc2.deposit(250.0);`
• `acc3.withdraw(100.0);`

Print all 3 balances on a single line: `Acc1: $0.0 | Acc2: $250.0 | Acc3: $400.0`.

practiceProblems.title: Account Transfer Operation
practiceProblems.description:
Final Capstone Challenge: Implement a transfer method between two collaborating bank accounts:

• Add method `boolean transferTo(BankAccount target, double amount)`:
  - If `amount > 0 && this.balance >= amount`:
  - Subtract `amount` from `this.balance`
  - Add `amount` to `target.balance`
  - Return `true`, else return `false`.
• In `Main`, transfer $200.0 from Priya ($500.0) to Rahul ($100.0).
• Print: `Transfer Success: true | Rahul Balance: $300.0 | Priya Balance: $300.0`.
